title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Runbooks, and Incident Review Standards
author: Ari Chen
body:
Summary

This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning guidance, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and canonical runbooks. It is intended as the single-source-of-truth for service owners and on-call engineers responsible for production reliability.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Overview:
- SLOs quantify user-facing reliability and are the primary input to prioritization and release decisions.
- An error budget is the complement of the SLO (allowed failure). When burn thresholds are exceeded, automated and manual mitigations are triggered.

Primary SLOs (examples applied to inference-api service):

| SLO name | Objective | Measurement window | Source | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Availability (inference-api) | 99.95% | 30d rolling | success ratio of HTTP 2xx over total requests (excluding synthetic/internal probes) | ~21.6m allowable downtime/month |
| Latency (inference-api - small prompts) | p95 < 150ms | 30d rolling | real-user requests filtered by token_count <= 512 | measure tail latency separately for hosted vs dedicated fleets |
| Model-load success (model-serving) | 99.9% | 30d rolling | model load/training job success events | targets for Dedicated/private may be stricter |

Prometheus/PromQL examples (measured by SLO team):
- Availability (success ratio):
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-api",status=~"2.."}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-api"}[30d]))
- p95 latency (ms):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference-api"}[30d])) by (le)) * 1000

Error budget governance:
- Error budget = 1 - SLO. For 99.95% availability, monthly budget = 0.05% of time (~21.6 minutes).
- Burn thresholds and actions (service-level):
  1. 0-25% burned: Normal operations; product releases can continue.
  2. 25-50% burned: Notify service owner; investigate recent deploys/traffic changes; temp mitigations allowed.
  3. 50-75% burned: Pause non-critical rollouts; require SRE consultation and on-call approval for changes.
  4. 75-100% burned: Halt feature launches; initiate fast mitigation plan (rollback, traffic shaping).
  5. >100% burned: All launches frozen; exec escalation and follow incident review process.

SLO ownership and dashboards:
- Every production service must have a documented SLO, a named SLO owner (on call rotation or service lead), and a Grafana dashboard showing: current SLO, burn rate (14d and 30d), top error contributors, and latency percentiles.
- SLO owners are responsible for verifying measurement correctness quarterly and during major infra changes.

2) Capacity Planning

Principles:
- Plan for the 95th-percentile sustained load plus a 30% headroom for bursty workloads unless otherwise agreed in contract/SLA.
- Capacity planning must consider: CPU/GPU utilization, network egress, memory (KV caches, KV cache warm-up), model KV cache size, and storage IOPS for model artifacts.
- For Dedicated and Private customers include contractual buffers (typical reserved capacity + 10% guardrail).

Capacity runbook (high-level):
1. Collect telemetry: 95/99 p95 QPS, CPU/GPU utilization, queue lengths, 95th tail latency per region (last 90 days).
2. Forecast: Run a 90-day forecast using weekly growth rate; include at least two growth scenarios (baseline and high-growth).
3. Headroom target: Ensure provisioned capacity >= forecast 95th percentile * 1.30.
4. Validate: Run load tests (k6/jMeter) with representative prefix caching patterns and model load.
5. Procurement/Scale action: Open request with cloud-ops (for hosted) or schedule maintenance/scale for Dedicated.

Capacity alerting thresholds (examples):
- GPU utilization (node average) > 85% for 10m -> paging to infra-op.
- Queue length (inference-queue) > 1000 pending for 5m -> page on-call.
- Cache hit ratio drop > 15% relative baseline -> alert to product and infra teams.

3) Reliability Initiatives

Typical projects prioritized when error budgets are consistently burned:
- Continuous batching improvements to reduce tail latency under load.
- Adaptive KV cache warming to reduce cold-starts after deployments.
- Autoscaler improvements: predictive scaling for scheduled events and traffic shifts.
- Circuit breakers at the routing layer to fail fast and preserve SLOs for core flows.
- Model quantization QA and rollout playbooks to ensure performance regressions are detected early.

Initiative tracking:
- Each initiative must have: objective (impact on SLO/EB), owner, success metric, rollout plan, and rollback criteria.
- House initiatives in the Reliability Initiative board (OKR-linked) and report monthly SLO impact.

4) Incident Review Standards

Classification and severity:
- Sev1 (P0): Customer-facing total outage or SLO breach impacting > 50% of traffic or > 5 minutes of continuous outage for critical endpoints.
- Sev2 (P1): Degraded functionality or latency regression impacting a subset of customers or key flows.
- Sev3 (P2): Single-customer issues, internal tooling failures, or minor degradations.

Post-incident review process (blameless):
1. Timeline: publish a timeline within 24h of mitigation.
2. Triage: initial triage note with preliminary root cause within 48h.
3. Postmortem: full postmortem published within 7 days for Sev1/2, within 14 days for Sev3.
4. RCA structure: summary, timeline, root cause (contributing factors), detection rationale, impact, mitigation steps, corrective actions, action owners and due dates.
5. Action item tracking: link actions to JIRA tickets labeled reliability/incident-followup; owners must update status weekly until closed.

Standard artifacts to include in every postmortem:
- PagerDuty incident id and on-call rotations involved.
- Key Grafana/Prometheus panels with time ranges and PromQL.
- Deployment/rollout IDs and hashes (git commit / release tag).
- Traffic/traffic-shift events and correlated customer reports.

5) Operational Tooling Expectations

Core tooling stack (standard set):
- Metrics: Prometheus (service metrics), Cortex for long-term storage.
- Dashboards & alerting: Grafana, Alertmanager.
- Logs: Loki (structured logs retained 30d for production).
- Tracing: Tempo / Jaeger for distributed tracing.
- On-call / notifications: PagerDuty.
- Runbook / docs: Confluence (this space) + runbook short links in PagerDuty playbooks.
- Capacity & infra automation: Terraform + ArgoCD for infra delivery; fleet autoscaling uses Karpenter / custom autoscalers.

Operational expectations:
- Every production service must expose standardized metrics: request_count, request_errors, request_duration_seconds_bucket, gpu_utilization, queue_length, cache_hit_ratio.
- Alerts must include runbook links and a minimum actionable context (what to look at, common mitigations).
- Dashboards should show SLOs, burn rates, top error logs, top traces, and capacity indicators in a single view.

6) SRE Runbooks and Playbooks (canonical examples)

Runbook: High tail latency (p95 > SLO)
- Symptoms: p95 latency exceeds SLO for 5m and burn rate rising.
- Immediate actions (0-10m):
  1. Check Grafana SLO dashboard and top contributing endpoints.
  2. Identify recent deploys (k8s events, commit ids).
  3. If a deploy correlates, consider quick rollback (kubectl rollout undo or ArgoCD rollback).
  4. If backlog/queue growth: scale workers/GPUs, open emergency scale request.
- Mitigation (10-60m):
  1. Apply circuit breaker for non-essential features (routing-service).
  2. Increase batching window temporarily as safe option.
  3. Instruct product to throttle non-critical customers if necessary.
- Post-incident: Run the incident review process and schedule capacity or code fixes.

Runbook: Partial model loading failures
- Symptoms: model-serving reports repeated 5xx on load; model unavailable for >=1 region.
- Immediate actions: verify model artifact integrity in S3/Blob; restart model-serving pod; check KMS for decryption failures; fall back to compatible model variant (configured in routing policies).

Ownership and Oncall
- Service owners: named in service README and SLO doc.
- Primary on-call: rotates weekly and is first responder for alerts.
- SRE escalation path: primary on-call -> SRE on-call -> infra lead -> engineering manager -> director of engineering (for Sev1).

Appendices
- Templates: Capacity planning spreadsheet, Incident postmortem template, SLO measurement checklist are linked in related_pages.
- Contact list: infra-ops@redwood, reliability@redwood, secops@redwood.

Change log
- 2026-10-30: Initial published version (Ari Chen).
- 2026-11-05: Clarified error budget burn actions and added capacity alert thresholds (reviewers: Priya Nair, Miguel Torres).

For questions or to request a review/update to a service SLO, contact the SRE guild or open a PR against the SLO registry repository.
